topic: HNSW vs IVFFlat pgvector index selection
question_text: A team uses Aurora PostgreSQL with pgvector to index about 500,000 document embeddings and wants the best balance of recall accuracy and query speed. Which pgvector index type should they choose?

options.text: Flat (no index) — exact but O(n) scan

explanation: HNSW (Hierarchical Navigable Small World) gives the best recall-to-speed tradeoff for corpora in the ~10K–1M range, building a navigable graph with sub-linear query complexity. A flat scan is exact but O(n) and impractical at 500K; IVFFlat suits very large datasets but needs a training/list-tuning phase and typically yields lower recall than HNSW at equal speed; B-Tree indexes scalar values, not vector similarity.
source_topic: pgvector HNSW vs IVFFlat index tradeoff

topic: Titan Text Embeddings V2 configurable dimensions
question_text: Which Amazon Bedrock embedding model lets you choose the output vector dimension (256, 512, or 1024) to trade retrieval accuracy against storage cost?
explanation: Titan Text Embeddings V2 supports configurable output dimensions of 256, 512, or 1024, letting you balance accuracy vs storage/latency. Titan Text G1 is a text-generation model (not embeddings); Titan Multimodal Embeddings uses fixed dimensions; Cohere Embed English is not a variable-dimension model on Bedrock.
source_topic: Titan Text Embeddings V2 configurable output dimensions

question_text: Using Titan Text Embeddings V2 for RAG, which input type should be set when embedding the USER'S SEARCH QUERY (as opposed to the documents being indexed)?
explanation: Titan Text Embeddings V2 supports distinct input types: use search_query for the user's question and search_document for content during ingestion. This asymmetric embedding improves retrieval quality. clustering is for grouping similar documents and classification is for labelling tasks — neither is used for the query side of retrieval.
source_topic: Titan V2 search_query vs search_document input type

question_text: A developer embeds text with Titan Text Embeddings V2 using normalize:true (unit-length vectors). What is the mathematical consequence, and which similarity metric is appropriate?

options.text: Vectors are scaled to unit length, so cosine similarity equals the dot product — use cosine similarity
Vector dimensions are halved — use Euclidean distance
All components become positive — use Manhattan distance
Near-zero dimensions are dropped — use negative inner product

explanation: Normalizing to unit length (magnitude 1) makes cosine similarity equivalent to the dot product between vectors, and cosine similarity is the correct metric (pgvector's <=> operator). Normalization is a scaling operation only — it does not change the number of dimensions, force positivity, or drop dimensions.
source_topic: normalize:true makes cosine similarity equal the dot product
